items.excerpt: Harriman House says The Everything Code by macro analyst Raoul Pal is a trade publishing first: the book was built with an AI model trained specifically on the author's own previously published material. The publisher frames it as an author-authorised 'AI-facilitated' workflow rather than ghostwriting.

Dr Alan Finkel, founder of Proudly Human and Australia's former chief scientist, argues AI delivers 'no economic benefits for the arts or the creative sector' and calls for stronger labelling and protections against AI-generated books.

As publishers sign LLM-training licences, microdeals and multi-territory rights deals, royalty and reporting transparency for authors is becoming table stakes. The piece argues rights systems, not goodwill, will decide whether AI licensing money reaches creators.

This week's international roundup: German children's publisher Carlsen sues OpenAI with author Marc-Uwe Kling and illustrator Astrid Henn, saying ChatGPT generates Das NEINhorn-like stories, illustrations and even print-ready files with a fake ISBN and the publisher's logo; Brazil's Publitik launches an AI-agent book-market intelligence platform.
A look at which publishing technologies — AI-assisted production, metadata and discovery tooling among them — are worth piloting versus scaling across a house's workflow.

Chris Reid argues that AI agents are becoming the primary readers of published content, and that decades of work on persistent identifiers and structured metadata mean publishers are already equipped to serve machine readers — if they design for them deliberately.

AI retrieval systems can surface an article but often can't say which version they used — preprint, accepted manuscript or version of record. The authors call for version-aware identifiers to keep AI-mediated reading trustworthy.

Ashutosh Ghildiyal names the real risk of AI in publishing as 'cognitive debt' — the gradual erosion of the human judgment that gives writing originality and integrity — and sketches how an adaptive publisher can spend AI capacity without incurring it.

Indie author Nigel George argues writers hold more power over AI's trajectory than they think: set explicit boundaries on AI use, defend human copyright, and treat the model as a very sophisticated calculator rather than a collaborator.

A Villanova University study found readers rated AI-generated stories higher than human-written ones while being unable to reliably tell them apart — though people with more AI expertise spotted the machine text more often.

Editor Mary Kole unknowingly edited two AI-assisted novels and now charges a 50% surcharge, publishing the exact contract addendum she uses. Editing machine prose, she argues, is reconstruction work — finding the humanity in 'soulless' text — not an editorial conversation.

Five of this year's Pulitzer winners disclosed AI use in their submissions across 15 journalism categories — the highest disclosure count since tracking began in 2024, and a signal of how fast AI-use disclosure norms are hardening for writers.

Reedsy co-founder Ricardo Fayet on how AI answer engines are replacing browsing as the front door to book discovery, and what authors must change about metadata, reviews and positioning to get surfaced when a reader asks an AI what to read next.
ALLi's Self-Publishing News for 13 August 2026 explains how the EU's new AI transparency rules — including watermarking and training-data disclosure — reach indie authors far outside Europe.

Jason Koebler argues Anthropic's plan to watermark Claude's text by subtly swapping word choices reveals how AI companies see language: as interchangeable tokens rather than deliberate craft decisions writers agonise over.

404 Media planted trackers in a rare-book shipment and followed it to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas where books are debound, scanned and destroyed — evidence of physical books being consumed as AI training data.

Spotify is rolling out AI 'Prompted Playlists' for audiobooks plus conversational search — you can speak or type a request and get recommendations and plot details — alongside better series tracking, pushing book discovery into chat.
